b: An SDR workflow is the repeatable process a sales development representative (SDR) uses to prioritize leads, follow up, qualify fit, and hand qualified meetings to an account executive (AE). In another context, the acronym can mean software-defined radio; readers looking for that technology can visit WebSDR or SDR-Radio.com.

A CRM-first SDR workflow keeps lead information, outreach activity, qualification notes, and next steps connected. With Sales Hub, SDRs can manage prospecting activities and follow-up within HubSpot’s CRM instead of relying on disconnected spreadsheets and reminders. Here’s how to organize the daily workflow, decide what to automate, and give AEs the context they need for qualified meetings.

An SDR workflow is the structured, repeatable process a sales development representative follows to move a lead from initial assignment through qualification and AE handoff. It includes six stages: prioritization, follow-up, qualification, handoff, logging, and reporting. The goal is to make each lead’s status and next step clear so the sales team can manage its pipeline consistently.

A CRM-first SDR workflow keeps contact details, engagement history, qualification notes, and next steps in one connected system. Sales Hub supports this process with lead management, prospecting, automation, and meeting-scheduling tools that work with HubSpot Smart CRM. Reps can review previous interactions before following up, while managers can monitor activity and identify leads that need attention.

Timely follow-up matters, particularly when someone has requested information. The 2007 MIT Lead Response Management Study, conducted with InsideSales.com, found that the odds of contacting a web-generated lead were 100 times higher when a company called within five minutes rather than waiting 30 minutes. The study examined telephone responses to web-form leads, so its findings shouldn’t be treated as a current benchmark for every SDR workflow. Teams should define response targets based on the type of inquiry and track whether they meet them.
The Core Stages of a High-Performing SDR Workflow

A high-performing SDR workflow connects six stages, from deciding which leads need attention to reviewing the team’s results. Each stage depends on accurate CRM records and the core SDR skills reps use to communicate, qualify leads, and manage their work.

Review your assigned leads and rank them by customer fit, buying intent, and the urgency of their requests. For example, a prospect who matches your ideal customer profile and has requested a demo may need attention before someone who downloaded a general resource.
Use recent engagement and existing commitments to refine the order. The goal is to give reps a clear starting point while ensuring that time-sensitive inquiries don’t sit unanswered.

Set a consistent, relevant follow-up process for leads who have expressed interest in your business. Record previous outreach attempts, determine the appropriate next step, and schedule follow-up tasks in the CRM.

Use email, calls, or other appropriate channels based on the prospect’s preferences and your team’s outreach policies. Adjust the cadence when prospects respond, request a different time, or ask you to stop contacting them.

Use a consistent set of criteria to determine whether a lead is ready for a sales conversation. Confirm the prospect’s needs, how your offering fits those needs, who participates in the decision, and the expected timeline.
Record what you learn in the CRM. A consistent qualification process gives SDRs and AEs a shared understanding of what makes a lead ready to advance.

Pass qualified leads to an AE with the information needed for a productive first conversation. Include the prospect’s goals, pain points, relevant stakeholders, timeline, previous interactions, and agreed-upon next step.

Confirm that the prospect wants the meeting, and make the CRM record the source of truth for the handoff. This helps the AE continue the conversation without asking the prospect to repeat information they’ve already shared.
Record each meaningful interaction in the CRM, including its outcome, new qualification details, and the next action and due date.

Consistent logging gives SDRs and AEs a shared record of the relationship. It also helps managers distinguish leads that need follow-up from those waiting on a response or no longer pursuing a conversation.
Use CRM activity and outcome data to monitor workflow performance. Track response times, follow-up coverage, qualified meetings, AE acceptance, and recurring handoff issues.

Review these results regularly to identify where the process needs attention. When the team records activity consistently and configures its reporting appropriately, managers can evaluate workflow performance without relying on separate spreadsheets for every update.
How to Prioritize SDR Work Inside the CRM

In Sales Hub, SDRs can use lead management tools to organize leads and work from CRM records rather than separate spreadsheets. Start by defining which leads match your ideal customer profile, then use engagement and urgency to decide who needs attention first.
Start with fit: Review the industry, company size, role, and other relevant information already available in the CRM. Identify which leads match the customers your team can serve.

Prioritize explicit interest: Give appropriate priority to relevant demo requests, meeting inquiries, and direct responses. A prospect’s request for a conversation provides a clearer reason to follow up than an email-open notification alone.
Account for timing: Review the last interaction, the prospect’s requested timeline, and any promised follow-up dates. Make sure recent inquiries and existing commitments don’t get overlooked.

Work from one queue: Where available, use the sales workspace’s prospecting queue to complete tasks and outreach activities. Sales Hub Professional and Enterprise support the prospecting queue, subject to the required seat and permissions.

Review priorities daily: Update lead status and next steps when prospects respond or their circumstances change. Recheck the queue so your team works from current information rather than yesterday’s assumptions.
For more guidance on researching prospective customers and identifying relevant opportunities, review HubSpot’s sales prospecting techniques.
How SDRs Should Qualify and Hand Off Meetings

Qualification frameworks help SDRs determine when a lead is ready for AE handoff. The SDR should establish that the prospect has a relevant need, meets the team’s qualification criteria, and wants to continue the conversation. The AE should receive enough context to understand what the prospect needs and why the meeting was scheduled.
Use a consistent process for every handoff:

Choose a qualification framework. Establish criteria that fit your sales process. For example, MEDDIC examines factors like the prospect’s pain points, decision process, and economic buyer. Use SDR training to help reps apply the criteria consistently rather than relying on individual judgment alone.

Require consistent handoff notes. Record the prospect’s needs in their own words, relevant stakeholders and their roles, expected timeline, decision-making process, and any known budget or authority information. Include outstanding questions rather than assuming the SDR has facts the prospect hasn’t confirmed.

Confirm interest before scheduling. Make sure the prospect meets the team’s qualification requirements and has agreed to the next conversation. Record what the prospect expects to discuss with the AE.

Hand off through the CRM record. Update the lead’s status and owner, record the qualification details, and identify the agreed-upon next step. Team messages can alert the AE to the handoff, but the CRM record should contain the information needed to prepare for the meeting.

Once the prospect agrees to meet, HubSpot’s meetings tool can simplify scheduling. SDRs can share an appropriately configured scheduling link that lets qualified prospects choose an available meeting time with the AE. This reduces scheduling emails while keeping the meeting connected to the sales process.
What to Automate in an SDR Workflow

Automation can help SDRs manage reminders, task creation, lead assignment, and reporting while keeping conversations and qualification decisions in human hands. Start with repetitive administrative work that follows clear rules, then decide which tasks genuinely benefit from automation.
HubSpot’s tools support different parts of this process, depending on your subscription, permissions, and configuration.
Research helps SDRs understand a prospect’s company, business needs, and relevant context before starting a conversation.

HubSpot’s prospecting agent can help research companies and prepare outreach based on relevant information. SDRs should review the research and proposed messages before using them, check that the details are accurate, and decide whether the outreach is appropriate for the prospect.
The goal is to reduce repetitive preparation without replacing the rep’s responsibility to understand the customer.

Consistent follow-up becomes easier when SDRs don’t have to track every reminder manually. HubSpot’s sales automation tools support sequences that can send scheduled emails and create follow-up tasks. For example, a sequence can send an appropriate initial email and create a reminder for an SDR to make a call or review the prospect’s response.
Reps still complete manual call tasks and personalize their outreach. Teams should also review sequence enrollment and stopping rules so follow-up remains relevant and respects prospect responses.
Automated lead assignment can help teams route new inquiries to the right owner without manually reviewing every incoming record.

HubSpot workflows can assign records using configured ownership rules or distribute them among eligible team members. For example, a team can route a contact to the SDR responsible for the relevant territory or use supported assignment options to distribute eligible records.
Before enabling routing, define ownership rules, review how existing account relationships affect assignment, and establish what happens when a lead cannot be assigned.
Reps need accurate meeting notes, but documenting every conversation manually can take time away from preparation and follow-up.

HubSpot’s call tracking software helps teams record and manage call activity in the CRM. For supported meetings, HubSpot’s notetaker can generate conversation summaries and suggest next steps when the necessary features are configured.
SDRs should review generated summaries, correct any inaccuracies, and confirm the next action before relying on the notes for qualification or AE handoff.
When activity and outcome data are recorded consistently in HubSpot, configured reports and dashboards can use that information without requiring reps to maintain a separate reporting spreadsheet.

Start by deciding which data points the team needs, such as lead response times, completed follow-up tasks, qualified meetings, and handoff outcomes. Configure the relevant CRM properties and reporting views, then review the results for missing or inconsistent information.
For additional examples of automating repeatable administrative work, see HubSpot’s guide to workflow automation.

Automation shouldn’t replace the SDR’s responsibility to conduct qualification conversations, assess ambiguous buying signals, or establish trust with prospects. Use it to organize the work and surface relevant information so reps can make better-informed decisions.
How to Measure Whether the Workflow Is Working

A useful SDR dashboard should show both the work reps complete and the outcomes that follow. Track these sales metrics to understand whether leads receive timely follow-up, qualification criteria are working, and AEs receive useful handoffs.

Response time: Measure the time between an inbound inquiry and the SDR’s first follow-up attempt. Track this separately from the time it takes to establish live contact. Review response times by lead source or inquiry type so different requests aren’t treated as identical.

Follow-up coverage: Calculate the share of eligible leads that receive the follow-up required by your team’s process. Account for leads that respond, opt out, or otherwise no longer require additional outreach.

Meeting acceptance rate: Track the percentage of qualified meetings handed to AEs that they accept as meeting the agreed-upon criteria. Divide accepted meetings by total meetings submitted for AE acceptance, using a consistent definition of acceptance.

Handoff quality: Review AE feedback and track how often meetings need additional qualification because the original handoff lacked required information. Look for recurring missing details, such as stakeholder context or the prospect’s timeline.
Dashboard visibility: Check whether managers can review assigned leads, completed activities, outstanding follow-up tasks, and meeting outcomes without requesting separate updates from each rep.

Review these measures together rather than judging performance by activity volume alone. For example, an increase in booked meetings is less useful if a growing share of those meetings fails to meet the team’s qualification criteria.

A high-performing SDR workflow connects prioritization, follow-up, qualification, handoff, logging, and reporting through a consistent CRM process. Start with clear lead priorities, agreed-upon qualification criteria, and complete handoff notes. Then automate key administrative tasks and use reporting to flag missed follow-ups or recurring issues. Sales Hub provides tools for managing these activities within HubSpot’s CRM, helping SDRs and AEs work from shared information as the team grows.
